world_behind.title: A father watching his descendants die
world_behind.text: Nephi describes the destruction of his own people as something he has seen, and verse 7 breaks the prophecy open with an exclamation about the pain of it. This is not a warning to strangers. He is naming the end of his own line and saying he watched it.

world_behind.title: Four generations of peace
world_behind.text: Verse 9 gives a span rather than a date: three generations pass in righteousness after Christ appears, and many of the fourth. The record's own history will run exactly that arithmetic, which is one of the places the volume checks its own prophecy against its own narrative.

world_behind.title: Buried writers, speaking
world_behind.text: Verses 16 through 18 use Isaiah's figure (Isa. 29:4) of a destroyed people speaking low out of the ground with a voice like a familiar spirit. Nephi applies it to a written record recovered after his people are gone, and he will quote the Isaiah chapter itself in full in the next chapter (2 Ne. 27).

world_behind.title: Churches, and getting gain
world_behind.text: Verses 20, 21, and 29 describe a religious economy: many churches, envyings and strifes, and men who preach to obtain money and reputation. Nephi is describing a future he has been shown, not a present he is living in, since his colony had one temple and no market for preaching.

world_behind.title: A string of questions with the same answer
world_behind.text: Verses 25 through 28 ask four times whether God has excluded anyone, and answer four times: nay. The form is a legal cross-examination that ends in acquittal for the accused, and the accused is everybody.

world_behind.title: The invitation's shape
world_behind.text: Verse 33 ends with an invitation before it ends with a conclusion: he inviteth them all to come unto him, and then all are alike unto God. Ancient covenant language usually runs the other way, defining the group and then addressing it. This verse addresses everyone and defines the group afterward.

words.text: The stalk left standing after a harvest, dry and worth nothing except as fuel. It appears twice in three verses for the proud and the wicked. The figure carries no cruelty in it: stubble burns because it is dry, and the chapter's judgment language keeps choosing images where the outcome follows from the condition.

Nothing, no price at all. Treated at 1 Nephi 19:7. Nephi says his people sell themselves for naught, which is worse than selling cheaply. The word makes the transaction absurd rather than tragic, and it lands in the middle of the passage where he says the pains of his soul do not change what he has seen.

A familiar spirit is not a friendly one. The term names the ghost a medium calls up, the voice that answers from underground, and Israel's law put the whole practice outside the covenant. Isaiah had thrown the phrase back at his people eight chapters ago, asking why anyone would "seek unto them that have familiar spirits" (2 Ne. 18:19) rather than to God. Nephi takes the outlawed sound and assigns it to a book: a voice out of the dust, whispering, with the Lord named as the power giving it speech. Jacob will use the same adjective in its ordinary sense a few pages later, telling the rich to be familiar with all (Jacob 2:17), a fair measure of how far the two senses sit apart.

The husk separated from grain at threshing, so light that wind removes it. Applied here to "their terrible ones" (v. 18), the people most feared. The verse pairs the image with speed, at an instant, suddenly, and the two together say that what looked solid had no weight in it.

The plural is doing work: not envy as a disposition but envyings as recurring events, things that happen between groups. It sits between strifes and malice in a list of what many churches cause. Nephi's complaint about religious multiplication is a social one at this point in the sentence.

The old word for the nations outside Israel, people with no covenant and, for most of their lives, no way to hear of one. In a sentence built of paired opposites it is the only item without a partner, and the verb it takes is its own: the pairs name people he does not deny when they come to him, while the heathen are the ones he remembers. Whether Nephi meant the difference or inherited the phrasing, the sentence has room in it for people the invitation never reached.

phrases.term: The words which he shall speak unto you shall be the law
phrases.text: The chapter opens by dissolving the question chapter 25 spent six verses on. When Christ appears, what he says becomes the law. The tension between keeping Moses and looking to Christ is not argued here; it is given an expiry date and a successor, and the successor is speech rather than a code.

Malachi's promise reads "the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings" (Mal. 4:2), an image drawn from the sky, and Nephi had used the healing half of it one chapter earlier. Here the word is Son. Whether the difference is a translator's choice, a hearing, or a deliberate reading, the effect is to move the sentence from metaphor to person.

phrases.term: The Spirit of the Lord will not always strive with man
phrases.text: The sentence comes from the account of the world before the flood, where God says "My spirit shall not always strive with man" (Gen. 6:3). Nephi applies it to his own descendants and adds the consequence: when the striving ceases, speedy destruction. He also adds his reaction, that this grieves his soul. The Genesis verse says nothing of the kind.

phrases.term: Speak unto them out of the ground
phrases.text: Isaiah's line about a fallen city whose "speech shall be low out of the dust" (Isa. 29:4) is turned into a description of a book. The dead speak, and what they say is written. It is the record's own account of what it is, given by a writer who knows his people will be the ones under the ground.

Two verses give the whole shape of the record's coming forth: written, sealed, withheld from those who dwindled, and eventually brought out. Nephi states it as prophecy before quoting Isaiah 29 at length in the next chapter, so his readers meet the claim in his own plain words first and the poetry afterward.

phrases.term: The greatness of their stumbling block
phrases.text: The Gentiles are described as lifted up in the pride of their eyes and stumbling over something large. What they have built is many churches, and what they have put down is the power and miracles of God. The stumbling block in this sentence is their own construction, a harder charge than unbelief.

phrases.term: The Lord God worketh not in darkness
phrases.text: The hinge of the chapter. Everything before it has been destruction and secret combinations; everything after it is a series of denials that God excludes anyone. The sentence functions as a rule for reading the rest: whatever is done in secret is not his, and his dealings can be examined.

Stated as the reason for everything he does, and the proof offered is that he lays down his own life to draw all men to him. The verse makes love the explanation rather than the result, and it puts the laying down in the same clause as the loving, so that the death is offered as the evidence.

phrases.term: Buy milk and honey, without money and without price
phrases.text: Jacob had closed his sermon with the same invitation in Isaiah's words, "come buy wine and milk without money and without price" (2 Ne. 9:50). Nephi substitutes milk and honey, the phrase for the promised land, so the free purchase and the inheritance are folded into one line. The arrangement in both verses is the same: nothing is charged.

phrases.term: Priestcrafts are that men preach and set themselves up
phrases.text: The definition Nephi's brother left unexplained fifteen chapters ago, when Jacob named priestcrafts as one of the two causes of the crucifixion. Here it is spelled out: preaching for gain and praise, and not seeking the welfare of Zion. The record supplies its own glossary, and this entry is one of the clearest cases of it.

A definition inside a commandment. God commands that all men have charity, and then tells them what the word means, which suggests the term was not obvious to Nephi's hearers either. Here the record glosses the word for the first time, and the gloss is what makes the commandment executable. Paul writes that without it "I am nothing" (1 Cor. 13:2); Moroni will devote most of a chapter to it and say the same.

The chapter's last claim, and it arrives after a list of every division that mattered: black and white, bond and free, male and female, heathen, Jew, and Gentile. Peter reaches the same conclusion after a vision, saying "God is no respecter of persons" (Acts 10:34). Nephi reaches it as the end of an argument about who is invited.

verses.label: v. 4–6
verses.title: A messenger formula stamped on three verses running
verses.text: The record closes verses 4, 5, and 6 with "saith the Lord of Hosts," and twice inside that span it repeats one image: "they shall be as stubble" at verse 4 and again at verse 6. The stubble and the burning day are Malachi 4:1, quoted under Malachi's name only much later, at 3 Nephi 25:1. Here the phrase arrives with a different attribution formula attached and no source named, and it is put to work on one people and one destruction, with a general last day nowhere in view.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: The prophecy interrupted by the man delivering it
verses.text: The record breaks the oracle to record its cost to the speaker: "O the pain, and the anguish of my soul for the loss of the slain of my people!" Two more breaks follow, at verse 10, "notwithstanding the pains of my soul," and at verse 11, "and this grieveth my soul." Three interjections in five verses. Verse 7 also records the speaker overruling himself in the same sentence, "but I must cry unto my God: Thy ways are just," so the record preserves both the objection and its withdrawal.

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: A forecast given as a count of generations
verses.text: The prediction is not vague about duration: peace "until three generations shall have passed away, and many of the fourth generation shall have passed away in righteousness." That is a number the record can be tested against, and it is tested, since 4 Nephi 1:14–22 walks the generations off one at a time and 4 Nephi 1:24 places the first failure in the correct one. A prophecy stated as arithmetic four hundred years before its subject is unusual in these books; the more common form gives conditions without a term.

verses.label: v. 15–16
verses.title: An Isaiah oracle turned to a new addressee
verses.text: The record takes the siege language of Isaiah 29:3 and the voice from the dust of Isaiah 29:4 and changes the person throughout. Isaiah has the Lord camp "against thee round about" and lay siege "against thee"; the record has him camp "against them round about" and lay siege "against them with a mount." Isaiah's "thy speech shall be low out of the dust" becomes "their speech shall be low out of the dust." The second person of the original addresses Ariel; the third person here addresses a people not yet in existence when Isaiah wrote, and the alteration is systematic, not occasional.

verses.label: v. 25–28
verses.title: Four questions, four identical answers
verses.text: The record puts the argument in catechism form: each of verses 25 through 28 asks whether the Lord has excluded anyone, and each is answered "Behold, I say unto you, Nay." What follows the fourth Nay is the general rule, "all men are privileged the one like unto the other, and none are forbidden." Verse 25 also quotes Isaiah 55:1 with one substitution, "buy milk and honey, without money and without price" where the King James text reads wine and milk. The change swaps in the standard formula for the promised land.

verses.label: v. 29
verses.title: A word given a definition on its only occasion
verses.text: The record names priestcraft seven times, at 2 Nephi 10:5, here, 3 Nephi 16:10, 3 Nephi 21:19, 3 Nephi 30:2, and twice in Alma 1. Only this verse says what it is: "priestcrafts are that men preach and set themselves up for a light unto the world, that they may get gain and praise of the world; but they seek not the welfare of Zion." The definition is behavioral, and what it turns on is motive; office and doctrine are absent from it. That is why Alma 1:12 can apply it to a man who holds no office at all.

verses.label: v. 33
verses.title: A closing list built out of paired opposites
verses.text: The final verse sorts humanity by three pairs and then dissolves the sorting: "black and white, bond and free, male and female," followed by "all are alike unto God, both Jew and Gentile." Four oppositions in one sentence, each named in order to be denied. The construction matches Galatians 3:28, which pairs Jew and Greek, bond and free, male and female; this verse keeps two of those three pairs, adds one of color, and moves Jew and Gentile to the end as the summary instead of the opening term.

chapter.title: Two halves joined by a rule
chapter.text: The first twenty-two verses are destruction, secret combinations, and grief. The last ten are invitation. Verse 23 is the joint: the Lord God works not in darkness. Everything after it follows from that one sentence, and the chapter is built as an argument.

chapter.title: The record describes itself
chapter.text: Verses 15 through 18 describe a record written, sealed, and speaking "low out of the dust," and verse 17 states its custody, "they shall be written and sealed up in a book, and those who have dwindled in unbelief shall not have them." 2 Nephi 27 then quotes Isaiah 29 at length on the same subject, so the plain statement comes first and the prophetic source second. That is the order used for the whole block: 2 Nephi 25 explains before 2 Nephi 27 quotes, as 1 Nephi 22 explained after 1 Nephi 20 and 21 quoted.oetry second.

chapter.title: Grief is left in the text
chapter.text: Verse 7 and verse 11 both record Nephi's distress at what he has seen, and neither is resolved. A writer working from a prophetic outline could have removed them. Their survival is part of what makes the chapter's later invitation credible.

chapter.title: The invitations are stated as refusals
chapter.text: Rather than saying God welcomes everyone, the chapter asks four times whether he has excluded anyone and answers nay. The rhetorical choice matters, because it addresses people who already suspect they are outside and answers the suspicion in its own terms.

chapter.title: Priestcraft is defined by motive
chapter.text: Nothing in verse 29's definition concerns authority, ordination, or doctrine. The test is what a preacher is trying to obtain, which is a test anyone can apply to himself and almost nobody can apply to someone else.

chapter.title: The last verse answers the whole book so far
chapter.text: Two Nephi has spent chapters on Jews and Gentiles, covenant lines, remnants, and who inherits what. Verse 33 collapses all of it: he invites all to come, and all are alike unto God. Nephi does not treat that as contradicting the covenant material. He treats it as its point.

applications.title: Watch how you take correction
applications.text: The righteous in this chapter are identified by hearkening to prophets and not destroying them. Ask how you handle correction that arrives through a person, especially one you did not choose.

applications.title: Say the just thing while grieving
applications.text: Nephi cries out about his pain and then tells God his ways are just, in the same breath. Practice holding both rather than waiting until the grief resolves to resume trusting.

applications.title: Notice when the striving stops
applications.text: The chapter's most frightening line is about withdrawal. Identify where you have felt the Spirit less lately, and ask honestly whether something in you has been declining the struggle.

applications.title: Check what you are building
applications.text: The Gentiles' stumbling block is their own construction. Look at what you have built in the name of faith, a reputation, a routine, an organization, and ask whether it lets God's power through or replaces it.

applications.title: Ask what you get out of it
applications.text: The definition is about motive: preaching for gain and praise while not seeking Zion's welfare. Take the most public thing you do for God and ask, honestly, what you get from it.

applications.title: Take the four denials personally
applications.text: Read the questions aloud with your own name in them: has he told me to depart, to stay out, to keep away from his salvation or his goodness? The answer each time is nay, and it is meant to be heard by someone who suspects otherwise.

applications.title: Pick one division
applications.text: Pick a division you actually notice in a room, and ask what would change in your behavior for one week if you fully believed the people on both sides of it were alike unto God.

questions.text: What do I know to be just that I am currently in too much pain to say?
What have I sold myself for, and would I call the price naught if I said it out loud?
Where have I stopped striving, and is the quiet I feel peace or withdrawal?
Is there anything in my religious life that only works in the dark?
What do I get out of being seen to serve?
If charity is love, is what I call charity actually that?
Which of the categories in this verse do I still, in practice, treat as a criterion?
